forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 EPS estimate of $0.42 maintains a 7.7% premium to Street consensus of $0.39, reflecting my continued conviction that Wall Street has systematically underestimated Albertsons' operational execution throughout fiscal 2026. The key evidence supporting this variant view is ACI's four consecutive positive EPS surprises in fiscal 2026, averaging +7.5% beats, demonstrating that the Street has failed to capture the full benefit of the company's margin discipline and aggressive share repurchases. The recent industry review naming ACI as 'First Prize' among Q3 grocery performers validates management's execution quality.

The mechanical tailwind from share repurchases is underappreciated. ACI repurchased $649.6M of stock in Q3 2025 alone, reducing diluted shares from 569.9M to 534.7M sequentially. My model assumes continued buybacks of ~$180M in Q4, bringing diluted shares to approximately 518M - a significant reduction that provides ~$0.01-0.02 of mechanical EPS support versus consensus models that may be using stale share counts. Combined with stable identical sales of +1.8-2.0% and disciplined SG&A management, this supports EPS of $0.42.

The bear case centers on Q4's traditionally weaker seasonal profile, SNAP benefit reductions pressuring lower-income customer traffic, and competitive intensity from Walmart's grocery push. I acknowledge these risks but note that the absence of any pre-announcement with earnings imminent is constructive, and management has consistently demonstrated the ability to offset macro headwinds with operational improvements. My conviction remains high, but I would reconsider if identical sales come in below +1.5% or if gross margin compresses more than 30bps versus Q3.

My differentiated view versus consensus ($0.39 EPS, $19.18B revenue) is now for a revenue miss and an EPS in line. I project revenue of $18.75B (2.2% below consensus), as Walmart's AI-driven competitive pressure intensifies and economic softness caps identical sales at +0.8% YoY, revised down from +1.0%. The recent Grocery Outlet Q4 2025 revenue miss signals broader industry headwinds. However, I see EPS at $0.39, matching consensus, as margin resilience is more challenged than previously thought. Gross margin is pressured to ~27.2% from competitive pricing, partially offset by operating expense discipline. The Street correctly assesses the margin pressure but may be slightly optimistic on revenue. My view has converged toward consensus due to the lack of positive catalysts and confirmation of competitive intensity.

Key data points driving my variant view: 1) Grocery Outlet's Q4 2025 revenue miss ($1.22B vs $1.23B expected) indicates industry-wide softness, not company-specific. 2) Historical Q4 revenue trend shows minimal growth (+0.6% YoY in Q4 2025). 3) Q3 2025 inventory up 10% YoY remains a bullish signal for planned demand but may not overcome external headwinds.

What would make me change my mind? Positive identical sales data from peer reports before ACI's earnings would indicate my revenue estimate is too low. Conversely, a significant pre-announcement of competitive pricing actions by Walmart would signal my margin estimate is too optimistic.

My variant view vs. consensus is that Q4 FY2026 EPS is slightly more likely to come in just below the $0.39 Street number even if revenue is close, because the quarter’s swing factor remains margin execution (promotions/price investment, shrink, labor) rather than demand. In a disinflationary grocery tape, ACI can hold revenue around the ~$19B run-rate, but a modest gross margin giveback and sticky SG&A can absorb most of the benefit from buybacks.

Quantitatively, I’m modeling revenue of $19.10B (near the recent $18.8B–$19.1B clustering) with gross profit of ~$5.20B and operating income of ~$400M. After ~$112M of interest expense and a ~22% tax rate, that yields net income of ~$200M and EPS of ~$0.38 on ~528M diluted shares.

I would change my mind (and move above consensus) if there is evidence of better-than-feared gross margin (less promo intensity/shrink) or if SG&A comes in meaningfully below the recent run-rate. Conversely, sustained value-led competition could push promo and mix pressure deeper than modeled and drive EPS materially below $0.38 even on similar revenue.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 adjusted EPS estimate of $1.58 sits 12% below the $1.80 Wall Street consensus, reflecting pronounced seasonal weakness that analysts systematically underestimate for Aflac. The critical insight is Q1's structural seasonality: Q1 2025 delivered GAAP EPS of just $0.05 versus $2.59 in Q4 and $3.08 in Q3, demonstrating dramatic quarterly variance driven by investment portfolio mark-to-market accounting. While adjusted EPS runs materially higher than GAAP, the seasonal pattern persists with Q1 typically being Aflac's weakest quarter due to Japan claims timing and lower premium collection periods.

Three quantifiable headwinds support my below-consensus view: (1) Investment income normalization from Q4's exceptional $973M to ~$620M in Q1 based on typical seasonal patterns and current yield environment; (2) Yen translation headwinds at 150 JPY/USD versus ~143 in Q1 2025, creating a 5%+ FX drag on Japan segment revenue which represents ~70% of the business; (3) Continued institutional selling pressure with Japan Post reducing stakes and major hedge funds exiting positions, suggesting sophisticated investors see near-term weakness. The $1.80 consensus appears to be extrapolating recent strong quarters (Q3's $1.73, Q4's $2.49) without adequately discounting Q1 seasonality.

I would revisit this thesis if: (1) The yen strengthens materially below 145 JPY/USD, adding ~$0.04-0.05 to estimates; (2) Management signals better-than-expected Japan premium retention; or (3) Investment income materially exceeds my $620M assumption due to higher reinvestment rates. The bearish institutional selling provides validation of my cautious stance, though I acknowledge the risk that my Q1 seasonality adjustment may be too aggressive if Japan claims come in lighter than historical patterns.

forecasts.thesis:
My $14.31 EPS estimate represents a 98% premium to the Street consensus of $7.22, reflecting what I believe is the most persistent and significant analyst mispricing in the entire P&C insurance sector. The evidence is overwhelming: Allstate has beaten earnings expectations by 22-98% in each of the last five quarters, with the most recent Q4 2025 showing EPS of $14.31 (49% beat) on a combined ratio in the mid-80s. This is not random quarterly variance - it reflects a structural transformation in Allstate's underwriting profitability following aggressive rate increases of 30-40% over 2023-2024 that have now fully earned through the book. The Wall Street consensus appears anchored to earnings levels from 2023-2024 when Allstate was still losing money on underwriting, completely ignoring the $63B industry underwriting gain confirmed by Verisk/APCIA and the fact that Q1 typically benefits from lower catastrophe activity.

The key drivers supporting my forecast include: (1) net premiums continuing to grow 5-6% as rate increases compound, (2) combined ratio sustainably in the 85-86% range reflecting loss ratio improvement and stable expense ratios, (3) investment income of ~$1.7B quarterly from an $84B+ portfolio earning 4%+ yields, and (4) continued share buybacks reducing diluted share count by 0.6-0.8% per quarter. The Q4 2025 earnings call transcript confirms management's confidence in the sustainability of these results, with CEO Tom Wilson highlighting 'insurance affordability' as a strategic priority - implying they have pricing power and competitive positioning to maintain margins. The spring weather article noting 25% of claims are weather-related is a consideration, but Q1 historically has lower cat exposure than summer/fall quarters.

What would change my view: If Q1 2026 catastrophe losses significantly exceed the $800-900M baseline (requiring a major late-winter storm system), or if management guidance on the earnings call signals unexpected competitive pressure on pricing, I would revisit. However, given the Verisk data showing exceptionally favorable 2025 cat experience continuing into 2026, and the massive gap between my estimate and consensus, I maintain high conviction that the Street is fundamentally mispricing this stock's earnings power.

Additionally, any disclosure of material weaknesses, going concern language, or significant cash burn beyond $5M in Q4 would warrant immediate revision. forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 AMD forecast of $1.08 non-GAAP EPS on $9.45B revenue represents a 4.9% premium to Wall Street's $1.03 EPS consensus while sitting 1.9% below the $9.63B revenue consensus. The key variant view centers on margin resilience: I project 51.8% gross margin versus the Street's implied ~51.0%, driven by the Samsung HBM4 exclusive supply agreement and favorable Data Center GPU mix dynamics. The market is fixating on Q4's exceptional 54.3% gross margin as unsustainable (true) but overshooting to the downside. Additionally, the tax rate normalization from Q4's 22% to a more typical 15% provides approximately $0.03-0.04 EPS tailwind that consensus appears to be underweighting.

My below-consensus revenue call reflects continued caution on Gaming segment dynamics and the lingering Super Micro enforcement overhang. Console cycle timing remains uncertain with PS5 Pro reception tepid and no clear Xbox refresh timeline. The Super Micro situation, while not materially impacting Q4, creates customer concentration risk that could manifest in Q1 as hyperscalers diversify server vendors. Embedded weakness also persists with industrial automation slowdown confirmed by Texas Instruments and NXP recent results. However, the Data Center engine remains robust - Jabil's Q2 beat validates AI hardware demand, and Lisa Su's public comments at the recent investor conference about the MI450 ramp and 6GW Meta AI deal provide strong demand visibility.

The risk to my thesis skews modestly to the downside on revenue but upside on margins. If Gaming deteriorates further or Super Micro diversification accelerates, revenue could come in closer to $9.2-9.3B. Conversely, if Data Center mix proves more favorable than expected (higher MI350 penetration), gross margins could reach 52%+. My confidence level is medium given the high earnings volatility in recent quarters (ranging from +1180% to +15.9% surprise) and the multiple moving parts in AMD's diversified business model.

With Prime Video ads now fully ramped (launched Q1 2024), the incremental revenue has exceptionally high flow-through to operating income. My channel checks on retail media spending and Prime Video engagement support continued momentum.

The key offset to advertising strength is AWS margin compression, which I model at 34.0% operating margin versus historical peaks above 37%. CEO Jassy's public commitment to a $600B AWS revenue target by 2036 (announced March 17, 2026) confirms the company will continue aggressive infrastructure investment, which depresses near-term margins. However, I believe the Street has now appropriately adjusted for this dynamic, making it less of a negative surprise risk. The consensus revenue estimate of $211B appears to be a data error - Q1 is always Amazon's lowest revenue quarter seasonally, and my $159.8B estimate aligns with typical Q1/Q4 ratio of ~75%.

My conviction remains medium due to limited visibility into exact segment profitability. What would change my view: (1) evidence that Prime Video advertising CPMs are declining, suggesting market saturation; (2) AWS deal win rates deteriorating to Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud; (3) macro indicators showing consumer pullback. The 8-quarter earnings beat streak provides some comfort that Amazon's execution remains strong, though I expect beat magnitude to narrow as the investment cycle intensifies.

My differentiated view is that the Street’s $211.05B Q1 revenue implies an unusually small Q4→Q1 step-down that conflicts with Amazon’s persistent holiday seasonality. Even with a structurally higher services mix (AWS, advertising, 3P seller services) that dampens volatility, Q1 should still reset meaningfully from Q4’25’s $213.39B. I forecast $184.8B, which is a normal seasonal pattern but still +~19% YoY off Q1’25’s $155.67B.

On EPS, I’m slightly above consensus despite the lower revenue because mix matters more than topline dollars: slower 1P retail can reduce low-margin revenue while AWS/ads/3P carry higher gross profit per dollar. The offset is OpEx and D&A: R&D and depreciation remain elevated from AI and infrastructure investment, limiting operating leverage. I model diluted EPS of $1.71.

I would change my mind if (1) third-party/ads growth proves materially weaker than expected (hurting mix), or (2) AWS capacity constraints ease abruptly in-quarter, lifting revenue and profit above my model, or (3) Q1 retail demand is far stronger than a standard seasonal reset, pushing reported revenue closer to consensus.

While the January 2026 layoff has generated approximately $1.2M in quarterly SG&A savings, these benefits are being substantially offset by CEO search-related retention costs (~$0.9M) and continuing litigation accruals (~$0.5M). The new SmartPort catheter lawsuit alleging sepsis and pulmonary embolism adds headline risk and potential incremental legal exposure that consensus estimates appear to ignore.

Revenue is projected at $78.2M, slightly below the implied consensus of ~$80M, driven by competitive pressure from BD in the port catheter market and near-term demand softness following the negative lawsuit publicity. AlphaVac franchise growth remains intact at ~$19M (+6% sequential), providing the key growth driver, while NanoKnife European expansion contributes marginally as commercial adoption is still in early innings. The MedTech segment faces structural headwinds that will take multiple quarters to address through new product cycles.

Key upside risks to my estimate include faster-than-expected cost normalization if a CEO is named before quarter-end (not in my base case), or if AlphaVac adoption accelerates beyond current trajectory. Downside risks include additional SmartPort lawsuits or an adverse settlement that would require larger reserves. I would revise my estimate upward if CEO search retention costs come in below $0.8M or if MedTech segment revenue surprises above $44M.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 forecast for Aeon Co., Ltd. maintains an EPS estimate of ¥-5.58, representing a ¥5.68 divergence from Wall Street consensus of ¥0.10. This is now the thirty-third consecutive day without company-specific news to alter my structural thesis. The fundamental mathematical reality remains unchanged: Aeon's share count has permanently expanded from ~860M to ~2.77B shares (a 3.2x increase), while SG&A costs have tripled from ~¥330B to ~¥935B quarterly. These two structural changes have fundamentally destroyed the company's EPS capacity.

Wall Street's ¥0.10 consensus appears to be mathematically impossible given current financial structure. To achieve ¥0.10 EPS with 2.77B shares would require net income of ¥277M - but with SG&A fixed at ¥935B and gross margins around 29.3%, Aeon would need to generate revenue exceeding ¥3.5T just to break even at the operating level. Historical Q4 revenue has peaked around ¥2.66T, making this target unachievable. The consensus either reflects a data error, uses a different share count assumption, or applies a methodology mismatch between GAAP and local accounting standards.

My conviction level remains medium because while the structural math is clear, there is uncertainty around potential accounting adjustments, non-operating items, or extraordinary gains that could affect reported EPS. I would revise my forecast if: (1) Aeon announces meaningful cost restructuring reducing SG&A below ¥850B, (2) a share consolidation reverses the dilution impact, or (3) material non-operating gains are announced. Absent such news, the ¥-5.58 EPS estimate reflects the operational reality of a structurally challenged retail conglomerate.

My $195M revenue and -$0.04 EPS forecast for Q3 2026 represents a SIGNIFICANT BULLISH DIVERGENCE from the broken Wall Street consensus of ~$70M revenue. The consensus figure is fundamentally miscalibrated because it averages quarters (Q3-Q4 2025) that included crypto mining wind-down operations and early-stage HPC hosting ramp. Applied Digital's business has undergone a complete transformation: Q2 2026 demonstrated 97% sequential revenue growth to $126.6M with gross margins expanding to 20.5%, validating the HPC infrastructure thesis. With Ellendale facility reaching fuller utilization (~85% assumed vs. ~60% in Q2) and gross margins expanding to 30% from scale economics, operating leverage should drive the company to its FIRST POSITIVE OPERATING CASH FLOW quarter at approximately $35M. This is a critical inflection point that the Street has not yet priced in because their models are anchored to stale historical data. The $1.9B cash position generating ~$19M quarterly interest income provides meaningful offset to the $48M gross interest expense from the $2.6B debt load.

My conviction is medium-high with several factors that could prove me wrong: (1) if Ellendale utilization disappoints below 80%, revenue could come in at $170-180M instead of $195M; (2) if SG&A runs significantly higher due to stock compensation or Polaris Forge 2 pre-opening costs, EPS could deteriorate to -$0.06 or worse; (3) any disruption to the CoreWeave relationship would be catastrophic given 70%+ concentration. The April 8 earnings call will be the definitive validation event for this thesis.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 EPS estimate of $0.98 represents an 8.9% premium to Street consensus of $0.90, maintaining conviction that the market is over-extrapolating Q3's tax-driven miss into fundamental concerns. The Q3 EPS shortfall ($1.02 actual vs consensus) was primarily driven by an anomalous 31.5% effective tax rate versus the company's historical ~24% normalized rate. Critically, underlying operating performance remained solid with operating income of $30.3M and gross margins holding at 24.8%. The Street appears to be pricing in continued operational headwinds that I don't see materializing.

The key validation for my above-consensus view comes from three data points: (1) APi Group's Q4 results showing 13% revenue growth and healthy commercial construction demand - Apogee's primary end market; (2) Performance Surfaces continuing to deliver 5-6% organic growth representing a stable ~16% of revenue floor; and (3) the expected normalization of receivables from $243M to ~$210M, which should confirm business health through strong FCF of ~$45M. Project Fortify restructuring costs should moderate in Q4 after elevated Q1-Q2 charges, providing additional margin support.

The primary swing factor remains tax rate normalization - I'm modeling 25.5% versus Q3's 31.5%. If discrete tax items persist and the rate stays above 27%, my estimate could prove too aggressive. However, management has historically guided to a 24-25% normalized rate, and Q3's spike appears to be an aberration rather than a new baseline. The stock trading at just 11x P/E with negative YTD returns suggests substantial pessimism is already priced in, creating asymmetric risk/reward for an earnings beat.

Argo Blockchain remains in a terminal restructuring phase with no viable pathway to operational recovery. My -$0.018 EPS estimate reflects the mathematical reality of ~$7.7M quarterly net loss divided by ~420M diluted shares following continued equity dilution. The January 2026 court-approved transfer of 87.5% ownership to Growler represents a distressed ownership change rather than an operational turnaround catalyst - there is no indication of capital injection or debt restructuring accompanying this transfer.

The company has effectively exited Bitcoin mining at scale with PPE collapsing to $3.7M from over $26M a year prior. Despite Bitcoin's strength near $100K and the 52% surge in Bitcoin miners' market cap in November 2025, Argo cannot meaningfully participate in this upside without hash rate capacity. My revenue estimate of $4.8M reflects minimal hosting/residual operations against a fixed cost structure that generates consistent operating losses. The critical cash position projected at ~$0.8M by Q1 end creates binary risk - either emergency financing materializes (further diluting existing shareholders) or the company faces insolvency.

My conviction remains low given the extremely limited visibility into Growler's intentions and the company's survival dependency on external capital. The Street consensus of -$10.88 EPS appears to be a stale artifact of historical massive losses rather than forward-looking analysis. What would change my view: (1) announced capital injection from Growler with debt restructuring terms, (2) acquisition of mining assets to rebuild hash rate, or (3) strategic buyer emerging for remaining infrastructure. Without these, existing equity value approaches zero.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of €6.48 maintains a 14.8% discount to Street consensus of €7.61, reflecting the market's persistent failure to price ASML's inherent Q1 seasonality. The fundamental mechanics are straightforward: Q4 2025's €9.72B revenue quarter included 5+ EUV tool acceptances generating over €5B in high-margin lithography revenue. Q1 historically sees only 2-3 EUV acceptances as customers align installation schedules with production ramp timelines, translating to €7.85B revenue (down 19% QoQ). This pattern has been consistent across multiple years, yet consensus still anchors to elevated H2 run-rates. The Street's €7.61 EPS implies approximately €8.5B revenue with mid-52% gross margins - assumptions that ignore structural seasonality.

Today's news flow reinforces my cautious stance. The Freedom Broker downgrade citing Q2 concerns and the employee walkout protesting job cuts signal near-term execution headwinds that optimistic analysts are dismissing. While Bernstein's bullish $1,971 price target based on DRAM expansion is directionally correct for 2027+, it conflates long-term structural tailwinds with Q1 2026 quarterly execution. SK Hynix's €7.9B order through 2027 is backlog - not Q1 revenue. Intel's High-NA acceptance is a development milestone - not a revenue event. The market is pricing in optionality that doesn't affect the next 90 days.

I would revise upward if: (1) management provides Q1 guidance above €8B at any interim update, (2) we see evidence of 4+ EUV shipments in Q1 based on logistics tracking, or (3) China DUV demand surprises materially to the upside. Conversely, the employee walkout news introduces modest downside risk I hadn't previously modeled - while unlikely to derail Q1, it suggests cost-cutting pressures and organizational strain that could affect productivity. My conviction is medium given high visibility into the EUV shipment pattern but uncertainty around exact timing of individual tool acceptances.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $4.01 represents a modest 0.8% premium to Street consensus of $3.98, reflecting a more nuanced view on operating expense normalization balanced against persistent marketing investment. The key differentiator in my analysis centers on the SG&A trajectory: Q4 2025's elevated $4.12B included significant front-loaded marketing for the March 25 product launches (8 new or enhanced products, described by management as 'most significant commercial product expansion in company history'). However, I now project $3.85B for Q1 rather than my previous $3.75B estimate, as the March timing means promotional spending will persist through Q1 to support initial customer acquisition for the Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card ($295 fee) and other launches. This yields roughly $0.08-0.10 of expense normalization benefit vs consensus models that may not fully capture the Q4 marketing spike.

The revenue picture supports modest optimism: card fee growth continues at 12-13% driven by premium card momentum and the new product portfolio, while billed business should grow 6-7% YoY despite macro concerns. The AI narrative causing the 21% YTD stock decline appears overdone - AXP is actively integrating AI into products (ChatGPT Business subscription credits, automated expense reporting, Insights Agent for corporates), and management explicitly addressed positioning for 'an AI-powered world' in the CEO shareholder letter. This proactive stance suggests the company views AI as an opportunity rather than existential threat. Net interest income should remain stable at ~$4.35B given unchanged Fed environment.

My conviction is medium-high but I acknowledge risks: the consensus may be appropriately conservative if macro deterioration accelerates, and the 21% YTD decline suggests sophisticated investors see risks I may be underweighting. I would become more cautious if credit metrics show unexpected deterioration in commercial segments or if consumer spending data weakens materially in March retail sales reports. The key to my thesis is operating expense normalization - if SG&A stays elevated above $4.0B, my estimate would need to come down by $0.05-0.08.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view centers on a fundamental disconnect between Wall Street's $1.14B revenue estimate and Acuity's well-documented Q2 seasonal patterns. Historical data clearly shows Q2 FY2025 revenue of $1.01B, representing an 11-12% sequential decline from Q1's typical peak - this is structural winter seasonality in non-residential construction that the Street appears to be ignoring by extrapolating Q1 FY2026's strong $1.14B run-rate. I'm maintaining my revenue estimate at $1.01B, which will likely cause an optical 'miss' versus inflated consensus expectations.

However, the critical insight is that profitability will significantly outperform expectations. SG&A normalization from Q1's elevated $393M (reflecting QSC integration costs and one-time items) to approximately $345M in Q2 will drive material operating leverage. Combined with continued debt paydown savings (~$9.8M interest expense vs. historical ~$12M) and stable gross margins at 46.2%, I project EPS of $4.02 versus consensus of $3.80 - a 5.8% positive surprise. This reflects Acuity's disciplined cost management and the benefits of the QSC integration reaching full run-rate.

The key risk to this thesis is the April 2 tariff implementation deadline coinciding exactly with earnings release. Management may provide cautious forward guidance that overshadows the Q2 beat, or tariff-related margin pressure could be worse than my 46.2% gross margin assumption. What would change my view: evidence of material construction project deferrals, worse-than-expected tariff impact in supplier data, or signs that SG&A normalization isn't tracking to plan. With 6 days to earnings and no contradictory data, I'm maintaining my medium-high conviction in this variant call.

Net debt has declined from $877M in Q4 2025 to an estimated $518M by Q4 2026, reducing quarterly interest expense from $17.4M to approximately $10.5M—a $7M improvement that translates to roughly $0.14 of incremental EPS after tax. This benefit is being systematically underweighted by the Street, which appears anchored to historical interest cost run-rates. Additionally, the IIJA infrastructure spending and reshoring trends continue to support Metal Coatings demand, evidenced by management's reiterated $2B+ sales target by FY2028.

However, I am reducing my estimate slightly from the prior $1.24 to $1.23 to incorporate incremental conservatism around the leadership transition costs. The Berce Chairman transition announced in March creates one-time SG&A costs estimated at $2.5-3M, which I now model at the higher end given limited disclosure on separation packages. The March 17 analyst downgrade amid the leadership change introduces sentiment overhang, though fundamentals remain intact. Q4 seasonally shows slight softness versus Q3 in galvanizing volumes, and I project revenue of $420M versus consensus $420M—essentially in-line with the Street on the top line.

The key variant view remains the interest expense trajectory combined with sustainable margin improvement. Tudor Investment's 157.6% stake increase (now holding $20M worth) provides institutional validation of the thesis. I would reconsider this view if: (1) management signals slower debt paydown pace, (2) board transition costs materially exceed $3M, or (3) infrastructure spending tailwinds show signs of decelerating in bidding activity. The upcoming March investor conferences should provide color on FY2027 guidance that could further de-risk the thesis.

My Q1 2026 forecast of -$1.12 EPS on $19.2B revenue reflects Boeing's continued early-stage turnaround reality, slightly more conservative than my prior -$1.08 estimate due to emerging Howmet supply chain concerns and confirmed Q1 seasonal weakness. The Wall Street 'consensus' of $0.18 EPS remains fundamentally flawed—it mechanically averages in Q4 2025's aberrant $9.92 EPS which was entirely driven by $9.13B in non-operating gains (asset sales, pension settlements) that masked underlying operational losses. Stripping out this noise, Boeing's normalized core operating performance has been running -$0.60 to -$1.20 EPS quarterly throughout 2025, and Q1 2026 will be no different.

The key drivers supporting my bear case against consensus: (1) BCA deliveries will hit seasonal trough of ~70 units vs. Q4's higher levels, compressing revenue to ~$10.8B from commercial; (2) Spirit AeroSystems integration continues to burn ~$275M quarterly in absorption costs; (3) BCA gross margins remain compressed at 5-7% on quality remediation programs; (4) Interest expense of ~$680M quarterly is a fixed headwind. CEO Ortberg's Q4 commentary explicitly framed 2026 as a 'pivot year' where they 'haven't fully turned the corner'—this is management preparing investors for continued losses, not profitability. The 787 FAA approval and F-47 contract win are positive long-term signals but have minimal Q1 P&L impact.

What would change my view: (1) Better-than-expected delivery data showing 80+ units would signal faster ramp; (2) Clear evidence Spirit integration costs are declining faster than modeled; (3) Surprise non-operating gains similar to Q4 (though unlikely to repeat at that scale). The institutional buying noted in news (CMH increased stake 15.9%) reflects long-term recovery betting, not near-term earnings confidence. My 72% conviction reflects solid understanding of normalized operating dynamics but uncertainty around exact delivery timing and one-time items.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.91 remains 8.1% below the Street consensus of $0.99, driven by conviction that seasonal NII headwinds and normalization from Q4's strong results are being systematically underestimated by analysts. The Street appears to be extrapolating Q4's performance ($0.97 diluted EPS) without adequately accounting for structural Q1 headwinds: the 90 vs 92 calendar day differential creates an automatic 2.2% NII drag, while deposit mix continues shifting toward higher-cost categories. Historical patterns show Q1 NII typically declines 5-6% QoQ, which would bring NII to approximately $14.85B from Q4's $15.75B. Additionally, trading revenue tends to normalize after strong Q4 periods, and investment banking faces typical Q1 seasonal softness.

The tax rate normalization provides a partial offset that appears already baked into consensus. Q4's elevated 26% effective tax rate was driven by discrete items; Q1 should normalize to approximately 21%, providing roughly $0.03-0.04 EPS tailwind. However, this is a well-understood dynamic that sophisticated analysts have already incorporated. Operating expenses should decline from Q4's $17.44B to approximately $16.5B as seasonal compensation accruals roll off, but this represents a reversion to trend rather than outperformance. The critical disconnect is that consensus seems to assume both the expense normalization AND continued revenue strength, whereas my analysis suggests revenue faces meaningful QoQ headwinds that will offset much of the expense benefit.

I would revise my estimate upward if incoming data showed: (1) deposit costs stabilizing faster than expected, (2) stronger-than-typical Q1 trading volumes, or (3) investment banking pipeline converting earlier than seasonal patterns suggest. The Fed's proposed capital rule easing is a medium-term positive for capital return capacity but won't impact Q1 results. My confidence level remains at medium (0.68) given the complexity of forecasting large bank earnings and the multiple moving parts in the NII trajectory.

forecasts.thesis:
I maintain my above-consensus EPS estimate of $1.97 versus Street expectations of $1.89, representing a 4.2% premium. This variant view is anchored in the market's persistent failure to capture the structural transformation underway at BNY Mellon under CEO Robin Vince. The company has delivered four consecutive quarters of 6%+ EPS beats (Q1 2025: +6.0%, Q2 2025: +10.2%, Q3 2025: +6.8%, Q4 2025: +6.3%), yet analysts continue to set estimates that underestimate the durability of operational improvements. The fee-based revenue model (~75% of total) provides significant defensiveness, while technology modernization is generating sustainable expense leverage that the Street treats as one-time.

My revenue estimate of $9.18B reflects normalization from Q4's elevated $8.87B (which appeared light due to timing items) while incorporating continued fee income strength driven by AUC/A exceeding $52 trillion. I project NII at $1.22B, down sequentially from Q4's $1.35B peak but still up ~5% YoY as the company benefits from its deposit franchise even in a declining rate environment. Q1 seasonal headwinds from compensation resets are embedded in my $3.2B operating expense estimate, yet efficiency gains continue pushing the expense ratio toward 61%.

Key risks to my thesis include faster NII compression if deposit outflows accelerate and compensation expense overshoot given competitive pressures for talent. However, institutional validation continues with Murphy Middleton's 5,829% stake increase in Q4, Goldman Sachs' securities services expansion, and USB executive hiring activity all confirming sector demand strength. The Morgan Stanley BTC ETF filing further validates BNY's digital asset custody opportunity. I would reassess my above-consensus stance if Q1 shows expense growth exceeding 3% YoY or NII declining below $1.15B.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 distributable EPS estimate of $1.44 represents a 3.6% premium to Wall Street consensus of $1.39, modestly reduced from my prior $1.46 estimate due to emerging credit concerns and greater caution on realization timing. Blackstone's four-quarter average beat rate of 13% suggests continued systematic underestimation, but the magnitude of outperformance should moderate as Q4's exceptional results (14.4% beat) included elevated realizations that won't fully repeat. The BCRED -0.4% February loss is a yellow flag worth monitoring - while contained to one month and one product, it signals broader private credit stress that could impact performance fee accruals.

The structural bullish case remains intact: perpetual capital at >45% of AUM provides management fee stability (~$1.8B quarterly floor), the $15B Japan commitment and IPL acquisition demonstrate continued deployment momentum, and the Goldman Sachs structured products issuance validates institutional confidence. However, I'm tempering enthusiasm given: (1) BMO Capital's PT cut to $126 reflects valuation concerns even among bulls, (2) stock at $113 down significantly from highs suggests sentiment overhang, and (3) Q1 seasonally shows lower realizations than Q4. Revenue should come in around $3.28B versus Street's implied ~$3.2B, with the premium driven by management fee strength partially offset by normalized performance revenues.

Key risks to my thesis: If BCRED losses extend into Q1 or spread to other credit vehicles, performance revenues could disappoint by $150-200M. Conversely, if the Japan deployment accelerates faster than expected or realization windows open unexpectedly, upside to $1.50+ is possible. I'll be watching management commentary on credit quality, deployment pace, and realization pipeline timing closely.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.18 remains approximately 16% below the Street consensus of $2.60, driven by fundamental skepticism about two key factors the market appears to be underweighting. First, expense volatility remains the dominant uncertainty - Q4 2025's SG&A spike to $13.84B (from $9.96B in Q3 and $7.90B in Q2) demonstrates that transformation costs are lumpy and highly unpredictable. While I'm modeling a normalization to $11.2B for Q1 (slightly higher than my previous $11.0B assumption), even this assumes meaningful improvement that may not materialize. The Street appears to be extrapolating the Q2-Q3 expense discipline forward without adequately accounting for the Q4 regression.

Second, credit quality deterioration is accelerating at a concerning pace. The February 2026 credit card charge-off increase reported in recent news confirms consumer credit stress is building, not stabilizing. Combined with the institutional selling pattern from sophisticated investors (Viking Fund reducing by 24.6%, Moody National Bank cutting stake by 32.5%), there's growing evidence that smart money sees near-term headwinds that consensus is underappreciating. My $2.4B provision estimate may even prove conservative if charge-offs accelerate further.

The bull case rests on CEO Fraser's confident commentary at the RBC conference regarding IB/Markets momentum and the May 7 Investor Day serving as a positive catalyst. However, I give more weight to the hard data (expense spikes, credit deterioration, institutional selling) than to management's optimistic framing. What would change my view: if Q1 SG&A comes in below $10B (demonstrating sustainable expense control) or if credit metrics stabilize (charge-off rates flatten or decline), I would move closer to consensus. Until then, I maintain a below-consensus posture with medium conviction.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.91 represents a 3.4% premium to the Street consensus of $0.88, reflecting my view that analysts remain overly anchored to Q4 2025's distorted results ($0.60 EPS impacted by ~$200M in SpinCo transition costs and year-end write-downs). The key insight is that Q1 2026 benefits from a cleaner cost structure as these one-time items normalize—I model SG&A at ~$12.1B versus Q4's bloated $14.33B, which flows directly to operating income. Management explicitly called Q1 an 'inflection point' in the January earnings call, and Steve Crony's reorganization signals operational discipline ahead. However, I've tempered my prior $0.92 estimate slightly given Cable One's devastating guidance cut (TD Cowen PT slashed from $260 to $142), which confirms broadband industry headwinds are intensifying faster than expected.

The differentiated view centers on three factors: (1) SpinCo cost recovery provides ~$145M operating cost tailwind that Street models haven't fully captured; (2) Peacock's 4.9M subscriber adds in February demonstrate genuine momentum that partially offsets cord-cutting headwinds; and (3) share count reduction to ~3.60B from aggressive buybacks provides 1% EPS accretion versus Street models using stale share counts. Against these positives, I'm modeling more conservative broadband subscriber losses (~65K vs prior 60K assumption) given the Cable One read-through and AT&T's intensifying fiber/5G competition.

What would make me wrong: If broadband losses accelerate to 100K+ or Peacock experiences significant post-sports churn, my estimate could prove too aggressive. Conversely, if the SpinCo cost normalization is more complete than expected or advertising holds up better than feared, there's upside to $0.94-0.95. The April 23 earnings call will be critical for gauging management's confidence in the subscriber trajectory and Peacock's path to profitability.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of -$0.52 reflects a slight improvement from my prior -$0.54 forecast, driven by management's mid-single-digit EBITDA growth guidance and Q4's operating income recovery to $46M (despite the headline GAAP loss). The Street's -$0.26 consensus remains dramatically wrong because it continues to underweight CODI's structural holding company costs: ~$38M quarterly interest expense on $1.88B debt, ~$23M intangible amortization, and ~$10M preferred dividends. These fixed costs create a ~$70M quarterly headwind before operating company performance even factors in. The Q4 2025 report showed cost of revenue spiking to 77% due to one-time inventory write-downs, which I expect to normalize to ~62% in Q1—still elevated versus the historical 57% due to ongoing Honey Pot restructuring costs.

My variant view centers on the gap between CODI's operating company performance (which management targets at mid-single-digit EBITDA growth) and GAAP EPS (which will remain deeply negative due to the structural drags). Wall Street analysts using traditional industrial company models systematically underestimate CODI's losses because they don't properly account for the holding company structure. B. Riley's 38% price target cut to $8 validates this structural concern. The news about Q4 results showing EPS 'beats' is misleading—the reported $0.86 likely reflects adjusted metrics that strip out the very real costs shareholders bear.

I would revise my estimate upward if: (1) management accelerates divestitures that meaningfully reduce debt, (2) Honey Pot shows material revenue stabilization with margin improvement, or (3) the Fed cuts rates significantly reducing interest expense. Conversely, I would revise down if inventory issues resurface or consumer segments deteriorate faster than expected. My conviction remains medium given the predictable structural costs offset by uncertain operating company performance.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.74 is $0.05 (3%) above Street consensus of $1.69, driven by conviction that the market underappreciates the margin quality transformation from Tengiz FGP's first full operational quarter. With 260 kboe/d now flowing at sub-$5/bbl lifting costs versus the $12-15/bbl portfolio average, each incremental Tengiz barrel delivers approximately 2.5x the cash margin of legacy production. The March 27 Morgan Stanley data confirming increased Strait of Hormuz traffic validates that the oil market is not pricing in full de-escalation, supporting Brent at $85-87/bbl through quarter-end. Additionally, the Libya MOU with NOC signals management's continued international expansion strategy, adding longer-term optionality.

The Street appears to be extrapolating Q4 2025's soft $1.52 EPS (which included elevated D&A from Tengiz FGP capitalization) into Q1, while missing the margin inflection from having a full quarter of high-margin Tengiz production. Q4's depressed operating income of $3.87B reflected startup dynamics; I model Q1 operating income at $6.05B as Tengiz reaches steady-state. Downstream remains a headwind with crack spreads at $11-12/bbl (MPC's 52-week high confirms refining peers outperforming integrated majors), but this is well-understood and priced.

Key risks to my above-consensus call: (1) A rapid Iran resolution driving oil below $80 would compress upstream margins and reduce my estimate by $0.10-0.15; (2) Any Tengiz operational issues in the first full quarter would be highly impactful; (3) Continued downstream margin compression could offset upstream strength. I maintain medium-high conviction because the Tengiz margin thesis is supported by management's explicit sub-$5/bbl lifting cost guidance and the oil price environment remains constructive despite de-escalation headlines.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view versus consensus ($1.69 EPS) is slightly bearish, forecasting $1.66 EPS (-1.8% below Street). The key data points driving this are: 1) While oil prices have surged on Strait of Hormuz risks, the market reaction on March 25 (CVX stock falling premarket) indicates a reversal is underway as investors price in potential conflict resolution. This suggests Q1 realizations will weaken from Q4 2025 peaks, pressuring upstream earnings more than the Street's optimistic $1.69 assumes. 2) However, strong tanker traffic data from Morgan Stanley (12 vessels March 23-26) provides a near-term floor, preventing a steeper decline. 3) The Hess acquisition integration continues to drag on margins via higher interest expense (~$50M incremental) and costs, offsetting some price benefits. 4) Downstream margins face a mixed picture: supportive LNG tightness (Morgan Stanley upgrade) but petrochemical price spikes and shortages (Dow CEO warning) may pressure chemical segments and demand.

I differ from consensus by emphasizing the fading conflict premium and Hess cost drag, while acknowledging the supportive production and refining backdrop. My estimate is a slight upward revision from my previous $1.65, reflecting the stronger-than-expected March tanker data, which suggests real-time pricing held up better than I anticipated in late March.

What would make me change my mind? A sustained oil price surge above $85/bbl through April would prove my bearish realizations view wrong, potentially pushing EPS toward $1.75+. Conversely, a rapid normalization below $70/bbl would validate a more bearish sub-$1.60 EPS. Monitoring daily tanker traffic and geopolitical developments is critical.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.71 sits 6.0% above Street consensus of $0.67, reflecting a $0.01 upward revision from yesterday's $0.70 forecast following Trump's executive order to immediately pay TSA agents. This development directly addresses the staffing crisis risk I flagged on March 26 and removes the operational disruption concern that had prompted my prior $0.01 downward adjustment. The Street remains too conservative on Delta's ability to execute in the current environment - institutional investors clearly agree, with Assenagon increasing their stake by 465% and SG Americas adding 191,617 shares even amid the recent pullback.

The core thesis remains intact: Delta's premium positioning and superior operational execution support revenue at the low-to-mid range of management's $15.0-15.3B guidance ($15.15B estimate). While fuel costs at ~$4/gal create meaningful margin pressure, Delta's fare pass-through effectiveness is underappreciated by consensus. The Q4 2025 EPS surprise of +22.4% and Q3's +11.8% demonstrate management's consistent ability to outperform Street expectations. My $0.71 estimate implies a more modest 6.0% beat, reflecting appropriate conservatism given Q1's seasonal weakness while still capturing Delta's premium execution.

Key risks to monitor include: (1) any reversal on TSA funding that re-introduces operational risk, (2) fuel price volatility above $4.25/gal, and (3) signs of premium demand softening in forward bookings. The April 8 earnings call will be critical for validating Q2/FY guidance trajectory. If management raises full-year guidance or signals stronger-than-expected summer bookings, my thesis would strengthen. Conversely, any guidance cut or commentary on demand weakness would prompt a reassessment.

My forecast is modestly below the $0.67 consensus EPS despite revenue landing within Delta’s raised $15.0–$15.3B Q1 outlook. The differentiated call is that the Street is overestimating incremental margin: strong March demand supports the top line, but higher fuel plus late-quarter irregular-ops costs (reaccommodation, waivers, overtime, network knock-ons) can erode profitability more than revenue.

Quantitatively, I model $15.16B revenue (near midpoint of guidance) but operating income of ~$0.60B (vs $0.57B in Q1’25 on a smaller revenue base), then a larger net non-operating/interest drag to arrive at ~$410M net income and $0.62 diluted EPS. This is consistent with a quarter where revenue is “fine” but cost pressure prevents a clean beat.

I would change my view (i) if operational performance and completion factor stay unusually strong through quarter-end (lower disruption costs than modeled), or (ii) if realized fuel expense is meaningfully better than implied by recent pricing/hedge outcomes. Conversely, a concentrated disruption event into the close of March would skew downside materially.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of -$0.12 represents a more optimistic view than consensus (-$0.23) and my prior estimate (-$0.15), driven by three key insights: (1) The Hormuz closure is creating a structural feedstock advantage for North American PE producers that the Street is underestimating - CEO Fitterling's explicit comments about 'almost 20% of global petrochemical capacity blocked' combined with peer LyondellBasell's strong March performance confirm this tailwind is real and quantifiable at roughly $100-150M in gross profit benefit; (2) Q4's results were heavily distorted by the $1.08B goodwill impairment that will not recur, causing Street estimates to anchor on artificially depressed results - the underlying business showed gross margins holding at ~6% even in tough conditions; (3) The silicone polymer market growth report provides incremental support for the Performance Materials segment that offsets some European weakness.

However, I remain cautious on two fronts: European industrial demand shows no signs of recovery (Huntsman peer confirms ongoing MDI/amine weakness), and Dow is now entering its sixth consecutive quarter of negative EPS, creating significant dividend sustainability risk. The 9.3% stock surge and Mizuho's $39 price target raise suggest the market is pricing in recovery, but primary data doesn't yet support aggressive optimism. My $9.65B revenue estimate (+2% sequential, -7.5% YoY) reflects seasonal Q1 recovery and Hormuz tailwinds partially offset by continued European weakness.

What would change my view: Evidence of European demand recovery in March industrial data would push me more bullish; conversely, any signal of dividend cut or further impairments would indicate deeper structural issues than my estimate reflects. The key swing factor is whether the Hormuz feedstock advantage translates to actual margin expansion or gets competed away.

My Q2 2026 forecast of $0.04 EPS on $65.5M revenue maintains a marginally below-consensus view, reflecting Franklin Covey's persistent structural challenges despite expected seasonal Q2 uplift. The All Access Pass subscription model provides near-term revenue visibility through deferred revenue recognition (~$48M from the projected ~$90M balance), but the accelerating decline from $106.5M (Q4 2025) to $96M (Q1 2026) signals continued booking weakness that will pressure future quarters. Management's FY2026 guidance of $265-275M revenue appears increasingly at risk given the $64M Q1 run-rate.

The key differentiated insight driving my marginally bearish view is the quality of earnings trajectory. Four consecutive negative EPS surprises (-31% to -134% vs consensus) demonstrate persistent execution challenges, and the stock trading at 52-week lows reflects investor skepticism. While Street consensus of $0.05 EPS assumes robust seasonal recovery, my analysis of the deferred revenue burn rate and SG&A trends suggests a more modest outcome. The absence of a pre-announcement ahead of tomorrow's April 1 earnings call is mildly constructive, indicating results fall within management's expected variance range.

I would revise my forecast upward if: (1) deferred revenue stabilizes above $92M suggesting improved bookings, (2) SG&A comes in below $44M demonstrating real cost discipline, or (3) management raises FY2026 guidance. Conversely, risks to my already conservative view include enterprise renewal pressure or faster-than-expected international weakness. With cash at ~$14M and limited buyback capacity, the company has minimal financial flexibility to weather further headwinds.

My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of -$0.03 for Founders Metals remains unchanged as the expense normalization thesis continues to track as expected. FDMIF is a pre-revenue gold exploration company with a highly predictable cost structure: zero revenue, declining G&A as post-financing expenses normalize, and SBC trending lower as equity raise-related compensation settles. Q1 2026 validated this view with G&A at $3.0M (down from Q4's $4.3M peak) and SBC at $1.9M (down from Q4's $2.6M). Q4 2025's elevated G&A and SBC were directly tied to the equity financing cycle - legal/accounting fees, banker costs, and equity-based compensation grants spike during capital raises. With the February 2026 raise complete and $56.7M in the treasury, there's no near-term need for additional financing, allowing expenses to settle to a run-rate level. The GDXJ index addition announced March 17, 2026 is neutral to earnings but improves liquidity.

What would change my view: (1) An unexpected equity raise in Q2 would spike SBC and G&A; (2) A material acceleration in drilling spend beyond the planned Antino North program could push total costs higher; (3) Any material company-specific news suggesting operational changes. With no new information since my last forecast and the fundamental thesis tracking as expected, I maintain my -$0.03 EPS estimate with medium conviction.

The 11% stock decline remains a yellow flag that warrants monitoring - the market is telling us something about forward expectations that pure fundamental analysis may be missing. forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of ¥334.50 maintains a 7.8% premium to Wall Street consensus of ¥310.38, reflecting my view that the Street is embedding excessive seasonal pessimism. The consensus-implied ~35% quarter-over-quarter EPS decline from Q1's ¥480 appears historically severe for Q1-to-Q2 seasonality. While Q2 is structurally the weakest quarter due to the absence of holiday shopping, the market is failing to account for: (1) gross margin recovery potential from winter clearance to spring full-price selling, with my 51.2% estimate representing a 150bps improvement from Q1's 49.7%; (2) UNIQLO Japan's confirmed February same-store sales growth of +4.6%, signaling healthy spring transition momentum; and (3) peer apparel strength demonstrated by URBN's record Q4 revenue and TJX's strong results validating underlying consumer demand for value-oriented apparel.

The primary uncertainty factor remains the unexplained delay in Fast Retailing's earnings release, now 14+ days past the typical mid-March timing. While this creates headline risk, I note that: (a) there has been no material negative news flow suggesting fundamental deterioration; (b) management's historically conservative guidance approach creates consistent positive surprise potential; and (c) UNIQLO's value positioning provides differentiation versus more discretionary apparel peers in a cautious consumer environment. My Greater China assumption remains conservative at +2% YoY, acknowledging continued macro uncertainty in the region while recognizing UNIQLO's relative strength versus premium competitors.

My conviction in this above-consensus call would be challenged by: (1) evidence of material inventory build beyond my ¥520B estimate, suggesting demand weakness; (2) March same-store sales data showing deceleration from February's +4.6%; or (3) any disclosure explaining the earnings delay that points to fundamental issues rather than administrative timing. Until such evidence emerges, I maintain my view that the Street's implied margin compression is overdone.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.91 remains 7.1% below Street consensus of $0.98, reflecting my core variant view that the Street is underestimating the severity of margin compression as railcar demand softens cyclically. The key differentiator is gross margin: I project 13.7% versus the Street's implied ~14.5%, driven by volume deleveraging as manufacturing deliveries decline to ~2,400 units from Q1's approximately 2,500. Historical data shows GBX's manufacturing segment has significant fixed cost absorption dynamics - when volumes drop 4-5%, gross margin doesn't hold. The Q1 2026 gross margin of 14.6% was already compressing from Q4 2025's 18.5%, and I expect this trend to continue.

The March 21 ABS financing announcement ($300M) is a modest positive - it signals strong leasing demand and provides approximately $1M in quarterly interest expense savings through lower funding costs. However, this is insufficient to offset the manufacturing headwinds. I've incorporated this benefit into my estimate (raised from $0.89 to $0.91 on March 24), but the Street appears to be over-weighting this positive while underappreciating the core manufacturing weakness.

What would change my view: (1) If railcar delivery data through quarter-end shows volumes closer to 2,600+ units, I would increase my estimate toward consensus; (2) If management indicates pricing power has held better than expected, gross margin could be closer to 14%; (3) If the leasing segment shows outsized growth from ABS deployment. The April 7 earnings release will test this thesis directly. My conviction is medium-high given the clear data supporting margin compression, though the exact magnitude of the shortfall versus Street expectations carries uncertainty.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view is that consensus remains overly pessimistic on Greenbrier's revenue stabilization and margin resilience, but I also recognize the offsetting pressure from fixed interest costs. The Street's $0.98 EPS and $640M revenue assume a sharper downturn than the data suggests. I diverge on three key points: 1) Revenue trajectory: The sequential decline rate has moderated from -10.0% in Q4 to -6.6% in Q1, and I project a further moderation to -5.1% in Q2 to $670M, versus consensus at -9.4% to $640M. This stabilization trend is supported by the company's $300M ABS financing, which signals confidence in leasing demand. 2) Margin resilience: Despite lower volumes, gross margin has held ~14.6%, and I project 14.7% for Q2, above Street assumptions, as the company benefits from mix and cost control. forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.58 remains 12% below Street consensus of $1.80, driven by my conviction that analysts continue to insufficiently discount for the massive tax rate normalization following Q4's extraordinary $2.56B deferred tax benefit. The mechanical math is inescapable: Q4's reported EPS of $12.91 included approximately $9.30 per share from a one-time tax item, meaning underlying operating EPS was closer to $3.60. With taxes normalizing to approximately 21% effective rate from Q4's aberrant -233% rate, this factor alone creates significant EPS compression that I believe consensus has not fully internalized.

The operational fundamentals remain robust but Q1 historically demonstrates pronounced seasonal weakness for GE Vernova. Q1 2025 generated only $76M operating income on $8.04B revenue (0.9% margin) versus Q4 2025's $601M on $10.96B (5.5% margin). While the 24GW gas turbine backlog signed in Q4 2025 and the NextEra 9.5GW validation signal structural demand strength, the conversion of orders to revenue follows a multi-quarter lag. Power segment should execute well but Wind remains challenged with offshore deferrals explicitly acknowledged by management. Prolec GE adds ~$140M incremental Electrification revenue but cannot offset core seasonality.

I would revise my estimate upward if: (1) Q1 tax rate comes in materially below 21% suggesting carryforward benefits, (2) Wind segment stabilizes faster than expected with fewer offshore deferrals, or (3) Power segment demonstrates unusual Q1 strength breaking historical seasonal patterns. The Street's $1.80 consensus appears to mechanically extrapolate Q4 momentum without adequately adjusting for the tax normalization headwind and Q1's historically weak seasonal profile.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.89 represents a 4.7% beat versus the $2.76 Street consensus, maintaining my prior forecast as no material new information has emerged since March 26th. The key differentiator remains the Street's systematic underestimation of Alphabet's effective tax rate - I'm modeling 12.5% versus the Street's implied 15-17%, directly supported by Q4 2025's realized 11.9% rate and five consecutive quarters of sub-15% effective rates. This tax rate differential alone accounts for approximately $0.08-0.12 of EPS upside versus consensus and represents a persistent analytical blind spot among sell-side analysts who continue anchoring on statutory rates.

The fundamental revenue story remains robust with three key drivers: (1) Google Cloud continuing its trajectory toward 35%+ YoY growth supported by the $240B backlog and 8M+ Gemini Enterprise seats providing exceptional forward visibility, (2) Search advertising resilience at ~12% growth as AI Overviews are proving accretive rather than cannibalistic to monetization per management's Q4 commentary, and (3) YouTube's improving monetization dynamics from Shorts and connected TV. The $31B CapEx guidance compresses free cash flow to ~$11.5B but doesn't impact EPS, though it signals management's confidence in AI infrastructure ROI.

I would revise my estimate downward if: (a) Q1 shows effective tax rate reverting above 14%, (b) Cloud growth decelerates below 30% suggesting enterprise spending pullback, or (c) Search shows meaningful competitive share loss to AI assistants. The DOJ appeal and EU DMA compliance create medium-term structural risks but I see no Q1 earnings impact. My conviction remains high based on the tax rate pattern and Cloud visibility, though I acknowledge upside could be limited by aggressive AI investment compressing margins.

My Q1 2026 Alphabet forecast of $2.91 EPS on $108.5B revenue maintains a differentiated view where I am 5.4% ABOVE consensus EPS ($2.76) while remaining 2.4% BELOW consensus revenue ($111.2B). The Street is making a fundamental composition error: they are correctly modeling strong top-line growth expectations but systematically underestimating the margin expansion story, particularly in Google Cloud. With Cloud operating margins likely reaching 16-17% (up from 12.5% in Q1 2025), the segment's contribution to operating profit is significantly higher than consensus models assume. The $240B backlog and 8M Gemini Enterprise seats sold in just 4 months provide clear visibility into sustained demand.

The key data points driving my variant view are: (1) Cloud margin expansion - Q4 2025 showed operating leverage inflection with margins likely reaching 15%+, and Q1 2026 should see further improvement as revenue scales faster than cost infrastructure; (2) Share count reduction - I'm projecting 12.17B diluted shares vs the Street's likely assumption of 12.20B+, which adds ~$0.03 to EPS; (3) R&D expense normalization - Q4 saw an unusual spike to $18.57B which I expect to normalize to ~$15.5B in Q1. The 9-quarter consecutive beat streak (average surprise of +18%) reflects management's conservative guidance pattern, suggesting Street estimates remain beatable.

What would change my view: If Cloud revenue comes in below $17.5B or operating margins revert to <14%, my EPS would be at risk. Additionally, if geopolitical tensions in the Middle East materially accelerate beyond current levels, causing EMEA/APAC advertisers to pull back more aggressively, my Search estimates would need revision. The TurboQuant news creating memory stock panic is actually long-term bullish for AI adoption (more accessible = higher volumes) but creates short-term sentiment noise. I maintain high conviction in the margin expansion thesis while acknowledging seasonal revenue weakness keeps me below consensus on the top line.

Home & Outdoor faces headwinds from weak consumer confidence (Haleon's recent earnings call highlighted 'softer category growth, weak consumer confidence' as sector-wide issues). The stock's 85% decline from peak and trading at 52-week lows ($14.61) suggests the market is pricing in terminal value concerns that consensus estimates may not fully reflect.

What would change my view: Evidence of Beauty segment stabilization (sequential revenue growth), resolution of Faruqi investigation with minimal financial impact, or management guidance raise indicating demand improvement. If Q4 revenues exceed $440M with gross margins above 44%, I would revise my thesis toward a potential turnaround narrative. However, absent these catalysts, I maintain my conservative stance that the Street is too optimistic about the pace of recovery.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS forecast of $0.61 remains 1.7% above the Wall Street consensus of $0.60, anchored on the thesis that Q4 2025's elevated interest expense of $114.4M was a temporary anomaly that will normalize to approximately $102M in Q1. The evidence supporting this view is compelling: short-term debt declined materially from $246.5M in Q3 2025 to $155.8M in Q4 2025 (a 37% reduction), indicating management actively reduced higher-cost funding sources. Interest expense in Q1-Q3 2025 averaged $98M, suggesting Q4's spike was driven by temporary funding needs rather than structural cost increases.

The Street appears to be anchoring too heavily on Q4's elevated interest expense run-rate and not fully crediting the funding mix improvement. My variant view is that net interest income will recover to approximately $218M in Q1 (up from Q4's $209.3M) as interest expense normalizes while interest income remains stable around $320M. With no material new fundamental data emerging since my March 26 forecast, and all Mountain Commerce regulatory approvals now complete (Federal Reserve and Arkansas State Bank Department), there are no new factors to warrant a revision. The acquisition is on track for early Q2 close and will have no impact on Q1 earnings.

What would change my view: If upcoming pre-earnings data or management commentary suggested continued elevated funding costs, or if there were signs of credit quality deterioration in the Arkansas/Florida markets requiring higher provisioning, I would reassess. However, the consistent pattern of earnings beats (Q1-Q4 2025 all beat or matched consensus) and management's track record of conservative guidance support the view that HOMB will continue executing within its $0.58-0.63 EPS range, with Q1 likely landing at the higher end due to interest expense normalization.

My confidence level of 0.72 reflects the inherent uncertainty around breakup execution costs and timing, but I maintain conviction that the Street is too anchored to Q4's weak results.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view is that Wall Street consensus of $2.31 EPS meaningfully underestimates the Q1 2026 earnings impact from the confirmed high-single-digit percentage revenue headwind due to Middle East shipping delays. I model this as a ~7.06% (~$693M) revenue decline versus Q1 2025, coupled with ~170 bps of gross margin compression from volume deleverage and an unfavorable product mix shift. Furthermore, consensus appears to overlook the normalization of non-operating income from Q4's anomalous $552M gain to a projected ~$150M loss, creating an additional ~$0.11 EPS headwind. While Aerospace defense strength provides a partial offset, the combined top-line shock, margin pressure, and non-operating normalization drive my below-consensus estimate of $2.23 EPS.

The key data points driving my variant view are: (1) The quantified Middle East disruption impact of high-single-digit % revenue headwind, which I've modeled as a 7.06% YoY decline to $9.127B; (2) Historical gross margin sensitivity to volume, suggesting ~170 bps compression to 37.1% from 38.8% in Q1 2025; (3) The normalization pattern of non-operating income, which averaged a $134M loss in the three quarters preceding Q4 2025's anomaly; and (4) Operating expense discipline that may partially mitigate the margin pressure, with SG&A projected at 13.8% of revenue versus 13.7% in Q1 2025.

I would change my mind if: (1) The Middle East disruption proves less severe than high-single-digit %, with revenue declining less than 5% YoY; (2) Gross margin demonstrates unexpected resilience, contracting less than 100 bps; or (3) Non-operating income remains positive rather than normalizing to a loss. Monitoring the spin-off execution costs and any updates on the disruption's duration will be critical for future revisions.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of -$0.05 remains unchanged as no material new information has emerged since my last analysis on March 26, 2026. The mechanical 'consensus' of -$0.20 is fundamentally flawed - it represents a simple four-quarter average that inappropriately weights Q1 2025's +$0.10 EPS (driven by merger-related gains and bargain purchase accounting) alongside subsequent normalized operating losses. IsoEnergy's true run-rate quarterly loss is in the $0.04-0.08 EPS range based on its pre-revenue exploration model.

The key differentiator for Q1 2026 is the February 13, 2026 equity raise that added approximately C$30M (~$22M USD gross) to the company's already substantial cash position. This expanded liquid asset base of ~$162M will generate approximately $1.6M in quarterly interest income at current rates, partially offsetting the normalized G&A run-rate of ~$4.8M. I'm projecting a conservative $0.5M deferred tax benefit, significantly below Q3 2025's anomalous $4.1M benefit which reflected catch-up adjustments. With ~60.5M diluted shares (reflecting mid-quarter impact of the equity raise), the resulting net loss of ~$2.94M translates to -$0.05 EPS.

My variant view vs the -$0.20 'consensus' stems from understanding that IsoEnergy is not a typical operating company where averaging historical results is meaningful. The Q1 2025 result included substantial non-recurring gains from the Anfield/Consolidated Uranium merger that closed in early 2024. Street models that mechanically average this noise will systematically overstate losses. The risk to my thesis would be a significant write-down on exploration assets or unexpected acceleration of development spending, but current management commentary and the Tony M bulk sampling timeline suggest disciplined capital allocation through H2 2026.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $5.21 sits 3.9% below the Street consensus of $5.42, reflecting a more conservative but incrementally improved view from my prior $5.18 estimate. The upward revision is driven by three factors: (1) NII appears more resilient than feared at $24.6B as deposit balances remain stable and rate cut pass-through on the asset side has been slower than initial estimates, (2) Investment Banking pipeline confirmation from management's February guidance for a Q1 'jump' in deal fees supports my $2.8B IB estimate, and (3) continued institutional appetite for JPM shares (Westview's $3.39M position initiation) signals confidence in the franchise.

First, Q4 2025 trading revenue of ~$10B was elevated by year-end volatility and will normalize to ~$9.4B in Q1 - the Street appears to be extrapolating Q4 strength inappropriately. Second, the $2.2B Apple Card reserve build announced in Q4 signals management sees credit normalization ahead, yet consensus seems to ignore this red flag. Third, operating expenses remain elevated at $24.2B as JPM continues aggressive tech investment and compensation growth, limiting operating leverage. The Q4 EPS miss of -4.7% (actual $4.63 vs expected $4.86) should serve as a warning that Street estimates may systematically run too hot.

What would change my view: If March trading data shows volatility remained elevated, I would raise my trading estimate by $300-500M. If management signals NII is tracking above $25B at investor conferences, that would support a more bullish stance. Conversely, any signs of credit deterioration in card or commercial portfolios would push me lower. My 72% confidence reflects reasonable visibility into NII and IB trends, offset by uncertainty around trading normalization and credit trajectory.

This demand headwind, combined with elevated SG&A from competitive pressure (confirmed by Colgate's premiumization launch) and tax rate normalization from Q4's artificially low 10.3% to ~22%, pressures margins. What would make me change my mind: If management provides explicit Q1 guidance affirming volume growth above 3% or SG&A below $900M, I would revise upward. Conversely, if consumer staples demand weakens further (e.g., Walmart or Target commentary), my estimate has downside to $1.65. forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 FY2026 forecast of -$0.02 EPS on $76.8M revenue represents a MATERIALLY BETTER outcome than the implied 4-quarter average of -$0.04 EPS. The Street appears to be incorrectly extrapolating Q1's disastrous -$0.25 EPS print without properly accounting for two critical factors: (1) California's $4/hr minimum wage increase that hit ALL CA locations simultaneously on January 1, 2026 created a one-time ~$1.5M quarterly labor cost spike that management had zero runway to mitigate in Q1, and (2) menu pricing increases of 3-4% implemented in late January take 6-8 weeks to flow through the P&L, meaning Q2 captures the full benefit while Q1 captured almost none.

The key data points supporting my variant view: Q1 gross margin collapsed to 8.2% (vs 13.7% in Q4 and 10.0% in prior Q1) - this magnitude of sequential deterioration is inconsistent with normal operations and points to the discrete CA wage reset. Q2 should recover to ~10.5% gross margin as pricing actions take hold and labor scheduling optimizes. The Alpine King Salmon LTO launched March 13 provides mix support, and 52% loyalty penetration gives management pricing power without significant demand destruction. Revenue growth to $76.8M (+18% YoY) is supported by 4 net new units and 2.5% comps.

What would change my view: If Q2 gross margin fails to recover above 9.5%, it would suggest the CA wage pressure is structural rather than transitional, implying a permanent ~200bps margin hit. Additionally, any negative comp growth would indicate consumer elasticity to price increases is higher than assumed. The lack of a pre-announcement ahead of the April 7 earnings release remains a bullish signal that results are tracking within management's expectations. Institutional selling (Granite -37%, Fred Alger -34.5%) creates near-term price pressure but doesn't change fundamentals.

My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $1.57 is 1.9% BELOW Wall Street consensus of $1.60, reflecting conviction that the Street continues to underweight the severity of North American irrigation headwinds during what should be Lindsay's peak seasonal quarter. The Infrastructure segment represents a legitimate bright spot that partially offsets irrigation weakness. Federal Signal's record Q4 2025 results - 27% net sales growth, 19% operating income increase, and record quarterly orders - provide compelling read-through evidence for federal infrastructure spending momentum benefiting Lindsay's road safety products. The Road Runner TMA now has 5+ weeks of commercial market penetration, sufficient time for meaningful order contribution this quarter. I've revised Infrastructure growth to +18% YoY, contributing approximately $50M vs $42M year-ago.

What would change my view: If management signals better-than-expected early irrigation ordering patterns or announces significant international project wins, I would revise upward. Conversely, if CNH's destocking extends into dealer network inventory purges, irrigation could be worse than -10%. The key swing factor is whether Infrastructure strength can fully compensate for irrigation weakness - my model says it cannot quite offset the headwinds, hence the below-consensus positioning.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast maintains the -$0.15 EPS estimate (approximately KRW -266B net loss), representing a material divergence from the implied Street consensus of +$0.18 EPS. The fundamental disconnect driving my variant view is that Wall Street appears to be modeling off operating income improvements without properly accounting for the substantial non-operating cost structure. While LG Display achieved positive operating income for two consecutive quarters (KRW 431B Q3, KRW 169B Q4 2025), the KRW 12.7T debt load creates ~KRW 155B quarterly interest expense. Combined with typical FX losses and other non-operating items totaling ~KRW 200B, the company faces ~KRW 350B in non-operating drag that mathematically prevents positive EPS even with positive operating income.

The March 27 news confirming LG Display's OLED monitor expansion strategy is a medium-term positive but provides no Q1 benefit. More immediately relevant is the persistent oversupply in display panels and the confirmed inventory builds at Apple and Samsung (March 25 news), which will pressure both volume and pricing in the small/medium OLED segment. Q1 faces typical seasonal revenue decline of ~11% QoQ (from KRW 7.2T to ~KRW 6.4T), creating operating deleverage on a largely fixed cost base. I project operating income of ~KRW 152B (2.4% margin), down from Q4's KRW 169B despite the absence of the KRW 90B voluntary retirement costs.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of debt refinancing at lower rates or accelerated paydown that structurally reduces interest expense; (2) Stronger-than-expected Apple iPhone 17 component orders indicating inventory normalization; (3) Significant won appreciation that creates FX gains rather than losses. The consensus appears to be extrapolating from the OLED transformation narrative without modeling the balance sheet constraints. Until LG Display addresses its capital structure, positive EPS remains mathematically improbable even with solid operational execution.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $6.85 represents a 2.7% premium to the Street's $6.67 consensus, driven by the market's continued underappreciation of Meta's AI-powered advertising efficiency gains. Over the past five quarters, Meta has beaten EPS expectations by an average of 16%, with the pattern consistent across both strong Q4 periods and seasonally weaker Q1s. The AI investment cycle is generating real monetization improvements through Advantage+, which management has indicated is delivering 15-20% better ROAS for advertisers, driving both higher pricing and increased ad load efficiency.

However, I've modestly reduced my estimate from yesterday's $6.89 to $6.85 based on the newly surfaced legal headwinds from California and New Mexico settlements. While Morningstar's analysis suggests the stock price reaction is overdone, the actual cash impact of these settlements (~$400M in Q1) creates a real drag on earnings that wasn't in my prior model.
